beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: We can pay with quarters, dimes, nickels, and pennies. Paying exactly means matching the price. Fewest means the smallest coin count.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: The cent sign means cents. Choose any number of each kind.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Choose a quarter: twenty-five cents, leaving sixteen still needed.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A dime adds ten cents, leaving six still needed.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Each penny is worth one cent.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: I need all six pennies. There isn't a shorter way.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Your payment is exact. Five pennies equal five cents.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Slide five pennies together. Trade them for one nickel. Keep the other penny.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: One nickel and one penny equal six pennies in value.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four coins pay exactly. Can three coins pay forty-one cents?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Without a quarter, dimes have the greatest value. Three reach only thirty cents.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A quarter is the greatest coin that fits, leaving the least still to pay: sixteen cents.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Another quarter is already too much.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two dimes make twenty, too much.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A dime and nickel make fifteen: one penny short.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Any smaller pair is farther away. Three or fewer cannot work, so four is the fewest.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: A bookmark costs twenty-five cents. Which set of coins is worth exactly twenty-five cents?

do.text: A bookmark costs 25¢. Which set of coins is worth exactly 25¢?

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Set *A* is thirty cents, too much.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Set *B* is twenty cents, too little.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Set *C* has five nickels. They make twenty-five cents altogether.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Set *C* pays exactly. Trade five nickels for one quarter: fewer coins.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Now try it fast. Thirty cents.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Quarter, nickel.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Two coins. Three dimes also pay, but that is three.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: My turn. Seventeen cents.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Dime, nickel, penny, penny.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four coins.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Sixty-five cents.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Quarter, quarter, dime, nickel.

beats.speaker: learner
beats.say: Four coins again!

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Five pennies slide together and trade for one nickel.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Twenty-five cents plus ten cents plus five cents plus one cent equals forty-one cents.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Four coins pay forty-one cents. Three cannot, so four is the fewest.

beats.speaker: teacher
beats.say: Match the price. For the fewest coins, choose the greatest value that fits what is still needed.
